standard.title: Democratic participation
standard.description: how Australians are informed about and participate in democracy
standard.prior_knowledge: Students know the key features of Australia's system of government including democracy, the Constitution, responsible government and federalism (AC9HC7K01), and the characteristics of Australia's democracy including freedoms of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement (AC9HC7K02). They can explain how values of freedom, respect, fairness and equality support social cohesion (AC9HC7K05). The gap this descriptor fills is the mechanisms by which citizens actually participate in and are informed about that democratic system — moving from structural knowledge to participatory knowledge.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how Australians are informed about and participate in democracy, including the range of participatory mechanisms, how those mechanisms have changed over time, and the role of media, interest groups and campaigns in shaping informed citizenship.

nodes.label: Forms of democratic participation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the main formal and informal ways Australians participate in democracy, including voting, contacting representatives, joining political parties, standing as candidates, using lobby groups, and taking direct action.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least three distinct forms of democratic participation with an example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the full range of formal and informal participatory mechanisms — voting, contacting elected representatives, joining parties, standing as candidates, lobby groups and direct action — explaining the purpose and context of each.
wider: Compare participatory mechanisms across different levels of government (local, state, federal) and how the opportunities available vary by level
Investigate digital and online forms of participation (e-petitions, social media campaigns, online consultations) and how these have expanded the participatory landscape
Examine how participatory mechanisms differ in Australia compared to another democratic country
nodes.hinge_reason: If students conflate different forms of participation or cannot distinguish formal mechanisms (voting, candidacy) from informal ones (lobbying, direct action), subsequent nodes about how government is formed and how influence is exercised cannot be grounded. This conceptual foundation underpins the analysis of electoral strategies and media influence in later nodes.

response_modes.reason: Students need to build a working repertoire of participatory forms before analysing how they operate. Invest time ensuring all major forms are understood with concrete examples — not just voting.

success_criteria: Can distinguish at least three distinct forms of democratic participation and describe the purpose of each
Can give a concrete example of each form they describe

nodes.label: Voting rights and the AEC
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how voting rights in Australian democracy have changed since Federation and describe the role of the Australian Electoral Commission as an independent electoral service.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one significant change to voting rights since Federation (e.g. women's suffrage, Indigenous enfranchisement) and state the key role of the AEC.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the progressive expansion of voting rights since Federation — including women's suffrage, the removal of property qualifications, and the enfranchisement of First Nations Australians in 1962 — and describe the AEC's role in administering elections independently of government.
wider: Investigate the significance of the 1967 referendum and the 1962 Commonwealth Electoral Act for First Nations Australians' political participation and what each did and did not change
Compare the AEC's role and independence with electoral authorities in another country to examine what features of electoral administration matter most for democratic integrity
Examine debates about compulsory voting in Australia — its history, rationale and ongoing contestation
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that democratic rights were not given all at once — and that independent electoral administration is a structural safeguard — is necessary for students to meaningfully analyse citizenship and participation debates later in this descriptor and in K06. A thin treatment produces students who treat democratic rights as natural and universal rather than historically contingent.

response_modes.reason: The expansion of voting rights is a rich set of cases — women's suffrage, First Nations enfranchisement, compulsory voting. Widening across these cases prevents students from treating one change as representative of all change.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The history of voting rights is pedagogically rich because it connects democratic theory to contested historical change. Widening across First Nations enfranchisement, women's suffrage, and compulsory voting allows students to examine how inclusion in democracy has been extended, resisted and defined differently across different groups.
success_criteria: Can explain at least one significant change to voting rights since Federation, identifying who was excluded before the change and what changed
Can describe the AEC's function and explain why electoral administration needs to be independent of government

nodes.label: Young people and political influence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify issues of concern to young Australians and explain different ways young people seek to influence political processes.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two issues of concern to young Australians and describe one way young people seek to influence political processes.
nodes.typical_width: Examine several current issues of concern to young Australians (e.g. climate change, cost of living, mental health, social justice) and investigate a range of strategies young people use to influence political processes — including petitions, social media campaigns, youth advisory bodies, protests and direct political engagement.
wider: Analyse a specific youth-led political campaign in Australia, evaluating which participatory strategies were used and what impact they had
Investigate formal youth participation mechanisms such as the Australian Youth Forum or Youth Parliament and what they can and cannot achieve
Compare how young people's political influence and voting age varies across democratic countries

response_modes.reason: Students relate to this node personally. Widening across multiple issues and multiple participatory strategies builds a more realistic picture of youth civic engagement — preventing reduction to a single issue or a single action type.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Young people's own political agency is personally motivating content. Width here — across different issues and strategies — builds civic self-efficacy and prevents the reductive idea that youth political influence is only through voting (which most Year 8 students cannot yet do).
success_criteria: Can name at least two current issues of concern to young Australians
Can describe at least one strategy young people use to influence political processes and explain how it works

nodes.label: Case study: citizen participation in political campaigns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse a case study of citizen participation in a political campaign, identifying the participatory strategies used and evaluating their significance.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one case study of citizen participation in a political campaign, identifying at least two participatory strategies used.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a significant case study of citizen participation — such as the Uluru Statement from the Heart — examining the participatory mechanisms employed, the issues driving participation, and the outcomes or significance of the campaign.
wider: Compare two case studies of citizen participation from different eras or different community groups, examining whether the same strategies are available and effective across different contexts

Investigate how First Nations Australians have engaged with democratic processes as both participants and advocates for change, examining the opportunities and constraints within the Australian democratic system
Examine a recent local or state-level citizen campaign and analyse what made it effective or ineffective

response_modes.reason: Case study analysis requires students to connect specific participatory actions to broader democratic principles — not just describe what happened. Invest in the analytical scaffold: what strategies, for what reasons, with what outcomes.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Uluru Statement from the Heart is a rich and contested case that connects democratic participation to First Nations political agency. Widening to other case studies allows comparison of how participatory strategies vary by context, community and era — building genuine analytical capability.
success_criteria: Can identify at least two participatory strategies used in their chosen case study
Can explain the significance of the case study in terms of democratic participation — what it demonstrates about how citizens can seek political change

nodes.label: Media, interest groups and informed citizenship
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how media, social media, political parties and interest groups shape citizens' understanding of issues and their choices, and describe strategies used to influence electoral behaviour.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one type of media or interest group influences citizens' understanding of political issues or electoral choices, with a concrete example.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how media, social media, political parties and interest groups shape citizens' understanding of issues, policies and political choices — and describe the range of strategies used to influence electoral behaviour, including advertising, opinion polls, political consulting firms and campaign messaging.
wider: Investigate a specific example of a media or social media campaign that influenced public opinion on a political issue, evaluating its techniques and effect
Examine the relationship between political advertising, opinion polling and campaign strategy in an Australian federal election
Investigate the role of disinformation and media literacy in democratic participation — how citizens distinguish reliable from unreliable political information
nodes.hinge_reason: If students do not understand how citizens' political understanding is shaped by external actors, they cannot critically evaluate democratic participation or develop the informed citizenship concept. This node is the analytical underpinning for active citizenship in S04 and argument creation in S05.

response_modes.reason: The range of influence mechanisms — mainstream media, social media, interest groups, political parties, advertising firms — is wide. Widening across these prevents students from thinking influence flows only from one source.

Students often accept that 'media influences people' without understanding the mechanism. Invest in the causal logic: what specific features of media/campaigns shape political perception, and under what conditions.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Media literacy and the mechanisms of political influence are transferable critical thinking skills with direct student relevance. Width across different influence vectors — mainstream media, social media, interest groups, advertising — builds students' capacity to identify and critique these mechanisms in their own environment.
success_criteria: Can identify at least two different actors (e.g. media outlet, political party, interest group) that shape citizens' political understanding and explain the mechanism each uses
Can describe at least one specific strategy used to influence electoral choices (e.g. advertising, opinion polls, campaign events)
